title: Handover, transport and ICU safety
summary: The non-technical skills that keep ICU patients safe: structured handover and escalation (I-PASS, ISBAR), a systematic daily round, safe intra- and inter-hospital transfer, oxygen cylinder planning, incident reporting and safety culture, and mass casualty triage — adapted for Indian ICUs.
authors: ICU 360 content team (AI-drafted, pending consultant review)

topics.title: ISBAR and structured handover
topics.summary: How to give and receive a safe shift handover (I-PASS) and how to escalate a sick patient to a senior by phone (ISBAR) — with scripts a junior can use at 3 am.

definition.text: Handover is the transfer of professional responsibility and accountability for some or all aspects of a patient's care. Communication failures at handover are a leading contributor to adverse events; structured tools reduce omissions.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.detail: Update the written/electronic handover list before the meeting: diagnosis, key events, current support (ventilator, vasopressors, RRT), pending results, and an explicit to-do list with times. Protect handover time and place; minimise interruptions.

steps.title: Use I-PASS for each patient
steps.detail: **I**llness severity (stable / watcher / unstable); **P**atient summary (diagnosis, events, plan); **A**ction list (who, what, by when); **S**ituation awareness and contingency ('if MAP <65 despite noradrenaline 0.3, then…'); **S**ynthesis by receiver (the receiver summarises back and asks questions).

steps.title: Sickest first, at the bedside if possible
steps.detail: Hand over unstable and 'watcher' patients first and, ideally, at the bedside so lines, drains, ventilator and the patient are seen together; confirm allergies, resuscitation status and family communication.

steps.title: Phone a senior with ISBAR
steps.detail: **I**dentify yourself, your role, the patient and location; **S**ituation — what is happening now and why you are worried; **B**ackground — diagnosis, key history, current treatment; **A**ssessment — vital signs, your interpretation (e.g. 'I think this is septic shock'); **R**ecommendation/request — what you need ('Please come and review within 15 minutes', 'Can I start noradrenaline?').

steps.title: Close the loop
steps.detail: Read back the instructions received, write them down with the time, and agree when you will call back or when the senior will arrive. If you remain worried, escalate again — or higher.

steps.title: Document
steps.detail: Record the handover/escalation, the plan and contingency in the notes; update the handover list.

tables.title: I-PASS mnemonic
rows: '54-year-old, scrub typhus with ARDS, day 3 ventilation, PEEP 12, FiO₂ 0.6'
'Repeat ABG at 2 am; chase blood culture; family update at 9 am'
'If P/F <100 despite PEEP 14, prone and call me'
Receiver summarises: 'So, unstable, ABG at 2, prone if P/F <100 — call you'

tables.title: ISBAR phone script (example)
rows: 'Dr Rao, ICU night resident. I'm calling about Mr S, bed 7.'
'His BP has fallen to 78/40 over 30 minutes and he is more drowsy. I'm worried.'
'Day 2 after laparotomy for perforation, on meropenem, noradrenaline 0.1 mcg/kg/min.'
'HR 128, lactate 4.6 from 2.1, drain output increased. I think he may be bleeding or have worsening sepsis.'
'I'd like you to see him now. Meanwhile I've sent Hb and cross-match and given 500 mL. Should I call the surgeon?'

redFlags.text: If you are worried, call — concern alone is a valid reason to escalate (state it explicitly: 'I am worried about this patient').
Any patient flagged as 'unstable' at handover needs a face-to-face review early in the shift by the incoming doctor.
Unclear resuscitation status, missing allergy information or unknown pending critical results are handover failures — resolve before the outgoing team leaves.

pitfalls.text: Handing over 'everything' as an unstructured story: key actions and contingencies get lost — use a fixed structure.
No synthesis/read-back by the receiver: misunderstandings are not detected.
Calling a senior without a clear request: always end with what you want them to do.

pearls.text: Write the contingency plans ('if X, then Y') — they are what the night team actually uses.
Use the same structure for nurse-to-doctor, doctor-to-doctor and inter-hospital referral calls.

algorithm.title: Escalating a deteriorating patient
algorithm.description: Using ISBAR to get the right help in time.

nodes.text: Patient deteriorating or you are worried
Peri-arrest or airway/breathing threat?
Call the emergency/code team now; start resuscitation
Quick ABCDE, vital signs, key results; start immediate treatment
Call senior using ISBAR with a clear request
Read back instructions; agree review time
Improving by the agreed time?
Document and hand over contingencies
Re-escalate (consultant/higher); repeat ISBAR

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Human working memory is limited; under fatigue and time pressure, unstructured verbal communication loses information. Hierarchy ('steep authority gradient') makes juniors hesitant to state concern or request action clearly; structured tools give permission and a script.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **I-PASS (Starmer, NEJM 2014):** handoff programme (mnemonic, training, faculty development, verbal and written handoff tool) across 9 US paediatric residency programmes. Medical errors fell by 23% (24.5 → 18.8 per 100 admissions) and preventable adverse events by 30% (4.7 → 3.3 per 100 admissions), with no increase in handoff duration.
- **SBAR/ISBAR** originated in naval/aviation communication and was adapted to healthcare (Kaiser Permanente; promoted by IHI) to standardise escalation calls.
- **WHO Global Patient Safety Action Plan 2021–2030** lists safe communication and transitions of care as core strategies.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Bedside vs meeting-room handover (patient confidentiality, time, noise).
- Electronic vs paper handover tools — benefit depends on design and training more than medium.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Indian ICUs often have high patient-to-doctor ratios and long shifts; a short, structured written handover sheet per bed works better than long verbal accounts.
- Mixed-language teams: keep key terms (drug names, doses, targets) in English and read back numbers.
- NABH accreditation standards expect documented handover processes in ICUs.

topics.title: Structure of the daily ICU round
topics.summary: A reproducible, systems-based ICU round with a FAST HUG-style checklist, daily goals, and line/catheter/antibiotic reviews — so that nothing preventable is missed and the whole team (and family) knows the plan.

definition.text: A structured ICU round systematically reviews each organ system, applies a preventive checklist and sets explicit daily goals understood by the whole multidisciplinary team.

steps.title: Collect data
steps.detail: Overnight events, vital-sign trends, fluid balance, ventilator settings and ABGs, drug chart and infusions, lab/microbiology/imaging results, nursing concerns. Calculate SOFA or the unit's severity score if used.

steps.title: Examine and present by systems
steps.detail: Neuro (sedation/RASS, delirium/CAM-ICU, pain), respiratory (mode, settings, P/F, SBT readiness), cardiovascular (MAP, vasoactives, perfusion, lactate), renal/fluids (urine, balance, creatinine, RRT), GI/nutrition, haematology/VTE, infection (cultures, antibiotics day number), lines/tubes, skin, mobilisation, family/goals.

steps.title: FAST HUG every day
steps.detail: **F**eeding, **A**nalgesia, **S**edation, **T**hromboprophylaxis, **H**ead of bed elevation (30–45° if ventilated), stress **U**lcer prophylaxis (if indicated), **G**lucose control. Many units add: spontaneous breathing trial, bowel care, indwelling catheter/line removal, de-escalation of antibiotics.

steps.title: Write explicit goals
steps.detail: Write today's goals on a daily goals sheet/whiteboard: targets (MAP, SpO₂, RASS, fluid balance), tests, procedures, consults, what must happen before discharge, and who updates the family. Ask: 'What is needed for this patient to leave ICU?'

steps.title: Line and catheter review
steps.detail: Is every central line, arterial line and urinary catheter still needed? Insertion date, site condition; remove what is not needed. Use insertion and maintenance bundles for CLABSI prevention.

steps.title: Stewardship time-out
steps.detail: Indication, culture results, day number, planned stop date; de-escalate or stop where possible.

steps.title: Summarise and communicate
steps.detail: Read back the plan for each patient; assign tasks with names and times; family update; document. Revisit at an afternoon/evening 'board round'.

tables.title: FAST HUG — what to ask
rows: Can we feed enterally today? Target calories/protein met?
Pain score? Analgesia first before sedation?
RASS target (usually −2 to 0)? Daily sedation hold?
Still indicated (ventilated >48 h, coagulopathy)? Stop when risk resolves
Ready for spontaneous breathing trial? Bowels open? Lines/catheters needed? Antibiotics narrowed/stopped?

tables.title: Daily goals sheet — minimum content
rows: What needs to happen to leave ICU?

redFlags.text: A patient who is 'not improving' after 48–72 h needs a structured re-think: diagnosis, source control, drug levels, complications, goals of care.
A rising SOFA score or rising vasopressor needs on the round = escalate the plan, not just 'continue'.
Never leave the round without a clear resuscitation status and documented family communication for every critically ill patient.

pitfalls.text: 'Copy-forward' notes that repeat yesterday's plan without reassessing.
Rounds that exclude nurses, pharmacists and physiotherapists lose key information and buy-in.
Continuing stress ulcer prophylaxis and urinary catheters long after the indication has gone.

pearls.text: In Pronovost's daily goals study, the proportion of residents and nurses who understood the day's goals rose from about 10% to over 95%, and ICU length of stay fell.
Simple checklists for line insertion (Keystone ICU project) cut catheter-related bloodstream infection rates dramatically and sustainably.

algorithm.description: A repeatable sequence for each bed.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Complex ICU care involves hundreds of daily actions; errors of omission (forgetting thromboprophylaxis, leaving unnecessary lines) are more common than errors of commission. Checklists compensate for cognitive load and variable experience.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **FAST HUG (Vincent 2005):** a mnemonic for key preventive aspects of ICU care; extensions (FAST HUGS BID) add spontaneous breathing trial, bowel care, indwelling catheters and de-escalation.
- **Daily goals (Pronovost 2003):** before/after study in a surgical ICU; understanding of daily goals by residents and nurses increased from <10% to >95%; ICU length of stay decreased (from 2.2 to 1.1 days).
- **Keystone ICU (Pronovost 2006):** in 103 Michigan ICUs, an evidence-based checklist intervention (hand hygiene, full barrier precautions, chlorhexidine, avoid femoral site, remove unnecessary catheters) reduced median CRBSI rates from 2.7 to 0 per 1,000 catheter-days, sustained at 18 months.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Checklist fatigue and 'tick-box' behaviour — effectiveness depends on culture and leadership.
- Family presence on rounds — improves communication and satisfaction but needs time and privacy.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- In many Indian ICUs, rounds are consultant-led with large teams; assign one person to read the checklist aloud for each patient.
- Antibiotic stewardship is critical given high carbapenem resistance (ICMR AMR surveillance) — include a daily antibiotic time-out.
- Bilingual family updates at a fixed time reduce repeated queries and conflict.

topics.title: Intra- and inter-hospital transfer checklist
topics.summary: Safely moving a critically ill adult to CT, theatre, cath lab or another hospital: is the trip worth it, risk stratification, team and equipment, a pre-departure checklist, monitoring in transit, and handover on arrival.

definition.text: Intrahospital transport moves patients within the hospital (to CT, theatre, cath lab); interhospital transfer moves them between facilities. Adverse events (equipment failure, desaturation, hypotension, line or tube dislodgement) are frequent and largely preventable with preparation, trained staff and checklists.

steps.title: Will the result change management?
steps.detail: Weigh the benefit of the test/procedure/transfer against transport risk; consider bedside alternatives (POCUS, portable X-ray). Combine trips (e.g. CT head and abdomen together). Obtain consent where possible and inform family.

steps.title: Risk-stratify and choose the team
steps.detail: Unstable or high-support patients (vasopressors, FiO₂ >0.5 or PEEP >10, recent intubation, raised ICP) need a doctor competent in airway management and resuscitation plus a critical care nurse; stable patients may go with a trained nurse. Minimum two people for any critically ill patient.

steps.title: Secure ABCDE before moving
steps.detail: Airway: intubate electively if it may deteriorate; secure tube; record depth; ETCO₂. Breathing: on transport ventilator for 10–15 min before departure with acceptable ABG/SpO₂. Circulation: two working IV lines, vasopressors running steadily on charged syringe drivers, spare syringes prepared. Disability: sedation and analgesia adequate; seizures controlled; spine protection if trauma. Exposure: warm, drains clamped/secured per surgeon, catheter bag emptied.

steps.title: Equipment and drugs
steps.detail: Transport monitor (ECG, SpO₂, invasive/non-invasive BP, ETCO₂), transport ventilator with alarms, self-inflating bag with PEEP valve and mask, suction, airway kit, defibrillator for high-risk patients, oxygen calculated for twice the expected time, emergency drugs (adrenaline, sedation, fluid), and the patient's notes/imaging.

steps.title: Call ahead
steps.detail: Confirm the receiving area/hospital is ready (CT slot, bed, lift held); doctor-to-doctor ISBAR call for inter-hospital transfers; agree the route and who to call for help.

steps.title: Read the checklist aloud
steps.detail: Run a structured pre-departure checklist (see table) as a team, just before leaving.

steps.title: Monitor and record
steps.detail: Continuous ECG, SpO₂, ETCO₂ and BP; observations recorded at least every 5–15 min; watch tubes and lines at every move (bed → CT table). Pre-plan responses to desaturation, hypotension and accidental extubation.

steps.title: Handover and document
steps.detail: Structured handover to the receiving team; transfer monitoring and infusions one at a time; document events and adverse incidents and report them.

Stable on low-dose vasopressor or NIV/HFNC, or stable ventilated with low support

tables.caption: Adapted practical categories; align with the unit's policy and the ISCCM position statement.

redFlags.text: Desaturation, hypotension or ETCO₂ loss during transfer: stop, hand-ventilate with 100% O₂, check DOPE (Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment), check infusions and lines.
A patient who is unstable on the ICU ventilator will be worse on a transport ventilator — stabilise first or reconsider the trip.
Raised ICP patients: keep head up 30°, avoid hypoxia, hypotension and hyper/hypocapnia during transfer — secondary brain injury is common in transit.

pitfalls.text: Moving to the CT table without assigning one person to hold the tube and lines: accidental extubation and line loss are common at transfer points.
Running out of syringe-driver battery or oxygen in the CT room — check charge and supply before leaving.
Disconnecting PEEP in a recruited ARDS patient by switching to a bag without a PEEP valve — rapid derecruitment.

pearls.text: Keep a dedicated, checked transfer bag/trolley in the ICU and audit it every shift.
Ask: 'Can this test be done at the bedside?' — POCUS and portable X-ray avoid many risky trips.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Transport exposes patients to changes in ventilation (circuit disconnection, transport ventilator performance, derecruitment), haemodynamics (interrupted infusions, movement, acceleration), temperature and monitoring gaps — on top of reduced staff and equipment.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **ISCCM position statement (2025):** Indian recommendations on intrahospital transport — planning, risk stratification, staffing, equipment, checklists, monitoring, documentation and quality indicators.
- **ACCM/SCCM guidelines (Warren 2004):** inter- and intrahospital transport — communication, personnel, equipment, monitoring.
- **Fanara 2010 (French recommendations):** adverse events reported in a wide range of transports (up to about two-thirds in some series); most are minor but serious events (desaturation, hypotension, arrest) occur; risk factors include high PEEP, sedation needs and fluid resuscitation before transport; checklists reduce events.
- **Droogh 2015 review:** inter-hospital transfers by specialised teams with standardised equipment are safer; transfers remain high-risk episodes.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Routine CT in unstable patients vs bedside imaging.
- Specialist retrieval teams vs referring team escorts in low-resource settings.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- In India, ICU–CT distances can be long with shared lifts; arrange a held lift and security escort.
- Advanced life support ambulances with transport ventilators are often private and variable in quality — inspect equipment yourself before departure.
- NABH standards require documented transfer policies; the ISCCM 2025 position statement provides India-specific guidance.

topics.title: Oxygen cylinder planning
topics.summary: How much oxygen is in a cylinder, how long it will last at a given flow or ventilator setting, how much to take for a transfer, and how to stay safe with oxygen — using Indian cylinder sizes and gauges.

definition.text: Medical oxygen cylinders store compressed gas; contents are proportional to pressure (Boyle's law), so a half-full gauge means about half the gas remains. Contents (L) ≈ water capacity (L) × pressure (bar).

steps.title: Identify the cylinder
steps.detail: Read the label: gas (medical oxygen — black body with white shoulder in India), size/type and water capacity (litres), and check the gauge. Indian medical cylinders commonly in use: small B-type (~10 L water capacity) and large D-type (~46.7 L water capacity, 'jumbo'), filled to ~150 bar (≈ 2,200 psi) when full.

steps.title: Calculate contents
steps.detail: Oxygen content (L) ≈ water capacity (L) × gauge pressure (bar). Example: B-type 10 L at 150 bar ≈ 1,500 L; at 75 bar ≈ 750 L. D-type 46.7 L at 150 bar ≈ 7,000 L. If the gauge reads psi, divide by 14.5 for bar; kg/cm² ≈ bar.

steps.title: Estimate consumption
steps.detail: Face mask/nasal: set flow (L/min). Non-rebreather: 10–15 L/min. HFNC or turbine ventilator blending with room/piped air: oxygen used ≈ total flow (or minute ventilation) × (FiO₂ − 0.21) ÷ 0.79; if everything comes from the oxygen cylinder, use the full flow — HFNC at 30–60 L/min drains cylinders very fast. Pneumatic ventilators: add driving-gas consumption (can be ≥1 L/min) to minute ventilation.

steps.title: Duration
steps.detail: Duration (min) = contents (L) ÷ consumption (L/min). Use the shared calculator. Treat the last ~10–20% as unusable reserve.

steps.title: Plan the transfer
steps.detail: Required oxygen = consumption × expected journey time × 2 (safety factor), plus at least 30 minutes extra. Take enough cylinders, check each is full, and carry a spanner/key and a spare regulator if needed.

steps.title: Handle safely
steps.detail: Secure cylinders in holders (never loose on the bed); open valves slowly; no oil/grease on fittings; no smoking/open flames; keep away from heat; check for leaks (hissing); close valve after use and record remaining pressure.

tables.title: Common medical oxygen cylinders in Indian hospitals (approximate)
tables.caption: Naming conventions differ from UK/US letter sizes (e.g. UK 'CD' 460 L, 'D' 340 L). Always read the cylinder label and gauge.

tables.title: Duration examples (full B-type ≈ 1,500 L)
rows: Pneumatic ventilator, MV 8 L/min, FiO₂ 1.0 (+1 L/min driving gas)
tables.caption: Halve the duration for a half-full gauge. Apply a ×2 safety factor for transfers.

tables.title: Worked example — inter-hospital transfer
rows: Ventilated, MV 10 L/min, FiO₂ 0.6, turbine ventilator → 10 × (0.6 − 0.21) ÷ 0.79 ≈ 5 L/min; round up to 6 L/min
One full B-type (~1,500 L) is marginal → take two B-type cylinders

redFlags.text: A cylinder gauge falling faster than calculated suggests a leak or higher consumption (HFNC, pneumatic ventilator) — recalculate immediately.
Running out of oxygen during transfer is a never-event: double the estimate and carry a reserve.
HFNC on cylinders drains them very quickly: 40 L/min empties a 1,500 L cylinder in under 40 minutes.

pitfalls.text: Assuming a UK 'D' cylinder (340 L) or Indian D-type (7,000 L) are the same — names differ; use water capacity and pressure.
Forgetting the ventilator's driving-gas consumption when using pneumatic transport ventilators.
Laying cylinders unsecured on the patient's bed — a falling cylinder can cause serious injury and valve damage.

pearls.text: Write the calculated duration and the time you must change cylinders on a sticker on the cylinder or bed.
For long transfers, a lower FiO₂ that still meets the SpO₂ target saves oxygen with turbine ventilators.

Estimate consumption (flow, or MV × FiO₂ ± driving gas)
Need = consumption × journey min × 2 + 30 min reserve
Contents = water capacity × gauge bar for each cylinder
Total contents ≥ need?
Add cylinders or larger cylinder; reduce FiO₂ if safe; avoid HFNC on cylinders
Secure cylinders, check valves/regulator, note change-over time

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Compressed oxygen behaves nearly as an ideal gas at cylinder pressures: volume at atmospheric pressure ≈ water capacity × (gauge pressure + 1 atm), simplified to water capacity × gauge bar. Liquid oxygen in hospital tanks is different (1 L liquid ≈ 860 L gas).
consultantNotes.evidence:
- Oxygen planning is part of every transport guideline (**Warren 2004**, **ISCCM 2025**): calculate requirement for the journey with a substantial safety margin (commonly twice the expected requirement plus 30 min).
- During the COVID-19 pandemic, oxygen supply failures in India highlighted the importance of knowing cylinder contents, consumption of HFNC/NIV, and hospital oxygen audits.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Optimal SpO₂ targets during transfer (avoid hyperoxia vs margin for safety).
- Use of HFNC during transfers (high consumption) vs NIV or low-flow devices.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Indian medical oxygen cylinders are typically black with a white shoulder/neck; industrial cylinders must never be used for patients.
- B-type and D-type nomenclature and capacities vary between suppliers — confirm with your hospital's supplier and record them on the transfer trolley.
- Many district hospitals now have PSA oxygen plants installed after 2021; transfers still depend on cylinders.
- Ambulance oxygen supply is frequently a single cylinder — check before accepting the transfer.

topics.title: Errors, incident reporting and ICU safety culture
topics.summary: What to do when something goes wrong: immediate patient care, disclosure, incident reporting, the systems (Swiss cheese) view of error, root-cause analysis, and practical safety tools — checklists, high-alert medication practices and a just culture.

definition.text: A patient safety incident is an event or circumstance that could have resulted, or did result, in unnecessary harm. A near-miss did not reach the patient. Reason's 'Swiss cheese' model explains how latent conditions (system weaknesses) and active failures (individual slips) align to cause harm.

steps.title: Make the patient safe
steps.detail: Treat the consequence (e.g. naloxone for opioid overdose, glucose for insulin error), call senior help, monitor closely. Preserve evidence: keep syringes, labels, bags, device settings and logs.

steps.title: Inform the consultant and be open
steps.detail: Tell the consultant in charge. Disclose to the patient/family honestly and promptly with the senior: what happened, what is being done, an apology, and what will be done to prevent recurrence. Document facts in the notes, without blame.

steps.title: Report the incident
steps.detail: Complete the hospital incident report (including near-misses and 'no-harm' events). Reporting is about learning, not punishment. Serious events (sentinel events) trigger urgent review as per hospital/NABH policy.

steps.title: Systems analysis
steps.detail: Use a structured review (root-cause analysis or similar): sequence of events, contributing factors (task, team, environment, equipment, organisation), why defences failed (Swiss cheese model), and actions with owners and deadlines. Feed back to staff.

steps.title: Use proven safety tools
steps.detail: Checklists (procedures, central lines, transfers, time-outs), standardised concentrations and pre-filled syringes, independent double-checks for high-alert drugs (insulin, potassium, heparin, opioids, vasopressors), tall-man lettering, separating look-alike/sound-alike ampoules, barcode/closed-loop prescribing where available.

steps.title: Care for the 'second victim'
steps.detail: Staff involved in errors often suffer distress; offer debriefing and peer support; a just culture separates honest error (console), at-risk behaviour (coach) and reckless behaviour (sanction).

tables.title: Types of error (Reason) and responses

Wrong drug choice from knowledge gap

rows: Remove concentrate from wards; premixed bags; infusion pumps
Write 'units'; insulin syringes; standard infusion 1 unit/mL
Concentration and rate errors; interruption at syringe change
Use 'mcg' not 'µg'; sedation targets; naloxone available

redFlags.text: Concentrated potassium chloride, insulin, heparin, opioids and vasopressors are high-alert drugs — 10-fold or wrong-route errors can kill; double-check every preparation.
Any wrong-patient, wrong-site, wrong-route (e.g. intrathecal vincristine) or retained-object event is a sentinel event: escalate immediately.
Do not alter or back-date notes after an incident — record a dated, timed factual addendum.

pitfalls.text: Blaming the individual and stopping there — the same latent conditions will cause the next error.
Not reporting near-misses: they are free lessons that reveal system weaknesses before harm occurs.
Treating checklists as paperwork: benefit depends on genuinely performing the checks as a team.

pearls.text: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist reduced death (1.5% → 0.8%) and inpatient complications (11.0% → 7.0%) across eight countries, including India.
'Stop the line': any team member should feel able to halt a procedure if they see a safety risk.

algorithm.title: After an error or adverse event
algorithm.description: Patient first, then disclosure, reporting and learning.

nodes.text: Error or adverse event recognised
Is the patient harmed or at risk?
Treat, monitor, call senior; preserve evidence
Inform consultant; disclose to patient/family with senior
Incident report (also for near-miss); document facts
Sentinel/serious event?
Formal root-cause analysis; notify per NABH/hospital policy
Implement actions, feed back to team, support staff

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Errors arise from the interaction of human cognition (attention, memory, fatigue, cognitive biases such as anchoring) with complex systems (interruptions, look-alike products, workload, poor design). Safety improves most when systems are redesigned to make the right action easy and the wrong action hard.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **Reason (BMJ 2000):** person vs system approaches to human error; the Swiss cheese model; high-reliability organisations expect error and build defences.
- **WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (Haynes, NEJM 2009):** 3,733 patients before and 3,955 after across eight cities (including New Delhi); mortality 1.5% → 0.8%, complications 11.0% → 7.0%.
- **Keystone ICU (Pronovost 2006):** checklist-based culture change abolished most CRBSIs.
- **WHO Global Patient Safety Action Plan 2021–2030:** seven strategic objectives including safety culture, high-reliability systems, patient engagement and learning from incidents.
- **NABH (India):** hospital accreditation standards include incident reporting, sentinel event review and medication safety.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Mandatory vs voluntary reporting; fear of litigation reducing reporting.
- Balancing a 'just culture' with accountability.
- Checklist effectiveness outside trial settings (e.g. Ontario surgical checklist study showed no significant mortality reduction).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Fear of blame and legal action (Consumer Protection Act cases) discourages reporting in Indian hospitals — leadership must visibly protect reporters.
- NABH-accredited hospitals must maintain incident reporting and sentinel event systems; ICUs should review incidents monthly.
- The Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI) accepts adverse drug reaction reports.
- Look-alike ampoules (e.g. different drugs in identical ampoules from generic manufacturers) are a common Indian latent hazard — segregate storage.

quiz.explanation: Console honest error; coach at-risk behaviour; sanction reckless behaviour.

topics.title: Mass casualty triage and ICU surge
topics.summary: When casualties outnumber resources: START and SALT field/ED triage, colour categories, the ICU's role in a hospital disaster plan (incident command, surge capacity, reassessment of existing patients), ethical critical-care triage and India's NDMA framework.

definition.text: A mass casualty incident overwhelms the immediately available local resources. Triage prioritises care to do the greatest good for the greatest number; categories are typically colour-coded: red (immediate), yellow (delayed), green (minor), black/grey (dead or expectant).

steps.title: Activate the hospital disaster plan
steps.detail: On notification of a mass casualty incident (MCI), inform the ICU consultant and hospital incident commander; follow the hospital plan (incident command system, roles, communication tree). Do not self-deploy to the scene unless part of the plan.

steps.title: Sort casualties quickly (START)
steps.detail: Can walk → **GREEN** (minor). Not breathing after airway opening → **BLACK** (dead/expectant). Breathing: RR >30, or radial pulse absent/CRT >2 s, or cannot follow simple commands → **RED** (immediate). Otherwise → **YELLOW** (delayed). Spend <60 s per patient.

steps.title: Or SALT
steps.detail: **S**ort globally (walk → assess last; wave/purposeful movement → second; still/obvious life threat → first). **A**ssess individually with lifesaving interventions (control major haemorrhage, open airway, chest decompression, antidote autoinjectors), then categorise: immediate, delayed, minimal, expectant, dead. **T**reatment/**T**ransport.

steps.title: Lifesaving interventions first
steps.detail: Tourniquet/pressure for major haemorrhage, airway, decompress tension pneumothorax, tranexamic acid within 3 h for bleeding trauma, damage-control resuscitation (permissive hypotension in penetrating trauma without head injury, early blood products), warmth.

steps.title: Create surge capacity
steps.detail: Identify patients who can be stepped down or discharged; cancel elective admissions; open surge areas (recovery, HDU) with ventilators and oxygen; call in staff per roster; check oxygen supply and blood bank stocks.

steps.title: Critical care triage if overwhelmed
steps.detail: Senior triage officer applies pre-agreed, transparent criteria (likelihood of benefit), reassesses all ICU patients regularly, documents decisions, and ensures palliative care for those not receiving critical care. Bedside clinicians should not make rationing decisions alone.

steps.title: Re-triage and records
steps.detail: Triage is dynamic — re-triage on arrival, after interventions and over time. Tag and register every patient (MCI number) to track location and identity; keep families informed through a designated desk.

doseCards.role: Bleeding trauma within 3 h of injury
doseCards.dose: 1 g over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h
doseCards.workedExample: Adult: 1 g (2 × 500 mg ampoules) in 100 mL saline over 10 min; then 1 g in 500 mL over 8 h. Do not start >3 h after injury.
70 kg: 50 mcg IV, repeat every 5 min to effect; monitor RR/SpO₂.

tables.title: Triage categories
rows: Life-threatening but salvageable with prompt intervention
Tension pneumothorax, airway compromise, haemorrhagic shock
Unlikely to survive given current resources / dead
Massive head injury with GCS 3, extensive full-thickness burns in resource crisis

tables.title: START at a glance
rows: Radial pulse absent or CRT >2 s

redFlags.text: Chemical exposure (e.g. organophosphate, chlorine, ammonia): decontaminate BEFORE entering the ED/ICU and protect staff — secondary contamination can close the department.
Uncontrolled external haemorrhage is the commonest preventable cause of death in MCIs: apply tourniquets/pressure during triage.
Children and pregnant women need adapted triage (JumpSTART for children) — do not 'under-triage' a quiet child.

pitfalls.text: Over-triage (labelling too many red) overwhelms critical resources; under-triage misses salvageable patients — re-triage repeatedly.
Running the ICU as usual during an MCI without reviewing existing patients for step-down — surge beds are created by discharges.
Poor patient tracking: unidentified patients and lost families — register every casualty.

pearls.text: Exercises and drills (tabletop and live) are the best predictors of an effective hospital response.
Expect the 'walking wounded' and self-presenters to arrive first and overwhelm the ED before the most injured arrive by ambulance.

nodes.text: Casualty at triage point
Able to walk?
GREEN — minor; direct to minor-injury area
Breathing?
Open airway (reposition)
Breathing after airway opening?
BLACK — dead/expectant
RR >30/min?
Radial pulse absent or CRT >2 s?
Follows simple commands?
RED — immediate; control bleeding, airway
YELLOW — delayed; re-triage regularly

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Trimodal trauma death: immediate (non-salvageable), early (hours: haemorrhage, airway, tension pneumothorax — the target of triage and lifesaving interventions) and late (days–weeks: sepsis, multi-organ failure — the ICU's long-term workload after an MCI).
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **START (Benson 1996)** is the most widely used field triage algorithm; based on walking, respiration, perfusion and mental status. Evidence for accuracy is limited (over- and under-triage are common).
- **SALT (Lerner 2008)** was proposed as a US national all-hazards standard after review of existing systems; adds global sorting and lifesaving interventions, and an explicit 'expectant' category.
- **CHEST 2014 consensus (Christian et al.)** on triage for pandemics and disasters: triage only when resources are truly overwhelmed after surge measures; use a trained triage officer/team, objective criteria and reassessment, with ethical oversight and palliative care.
- **NDMA 2007 guidelines (India):** hospital disaster plans, incident command, surge capacity, communication, CBRN preparedness, mass-casualty drills.
- **CRASH-2 (2010):** tranexamic acid within 3 h reduced all-cause mortality in bleeding trauma patients (14.5% vs 16.0%) and death due to bleeding.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Use of SOFA-based scores for ICU triage (poor discrimination in some settings, e.g. COVID-19).
- Age or comorbidity cut-offs in triage (ethically contentious).
- Which field triage system performs best — no system is clearly superior.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- India's frequent MCIs include road and rail accidents, building collapses, stampedes, industrial chemical releases (e.g. Bhopal 1984, Vizag styrene 2020), floods, cyclones and terror attacks.
- **NDMA guidelines** require hospital disaster management plans; NABH standards also expect disaster preparedness and drills.
- Mass organophosphate/chemical exposures need decontamination areas and large atropine stocks.
- Use the '108' emergency services and district control rooms for coordination; designate one hospital spokesperson.

drugs.name: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine)
drugs.indications: Maintaining MAP during transfer of a shocked patient
drugs.adultDose: 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min IV infusion titrated to MAP ≥65 mmHg (or individual target).
drugs.preparationIndia: 2 mg/2 mL ampoules (check base vs bitartrate labelling); 4 mg in 50 mL = 80 mcg/mL; 8 mg in 50 mL = 160 mcg/mL. For transfer, carry a second pre-filled syringe.
drugs.cautions: Interruption during syringe change or line kinks causes abrupt hypotension — 'double-pump' or change syringes before departure.
drugs.monitoring: Continuous arterial BP during transfer when on vasopressors.

drugs.name: Propofol
drugs.indications: Sedation of ventilated patients during transfer
drugs.adultDose: Infusion 0.5–4 mg/kg/h (1% = 10 mg/mL); boluses 10–20 mg for procedures.
drugs.preparationIndia: 1% (10 mg/mL) 20 mL ampoules and 50 mL vials; use undiluted in a 50 mL syringe.
drugs.cautions: Hypotension (especially in hypovolaemia), propofol infusion syndrome at high doses for prolonged periods; lipid load.
drugs.monitoring: BP, sedation score (RASS), triglycerides with prolonged use.

drugs.name: Fentanyl
drugs.indications: Analgesia/sedation during transfer and for injured patients
drugs.adultDose: Boluses 25–100 mcg IV; infusion 25–200 mcg/h (about 0.5–2 mcg/kg/h).
drugs.preparationIndia: 50 mcg/mL ampoules (2 mL, 10 mL); common infusion 500 mcg in 50 mL (10 mcg/mL) or undiluted 50 mcg/mL.
drugs.cautions: Respiratory depression in non-ventilated patients, chest-wall rigidity with rapid large boluses, accumulation in hepatic failure.
drugs.monitoring: RR, SpO₂, ETCO₂, pain and sedation scores.

drugs.name: Midazolam
drugs.indications: Seizure control; short-term sedation when propofol unsuitable
drugs.adultDose: Seizures: 10 mg IM or 5–10 mg IV (0.1–0.2 mg/kg). Sedation boluses 1–2 mg IV; infusion 1–5 mg/h (avoid prolonged infusion where possible).
drugs.preparationIndia: 1 mg/mL and 5 mg/mL ampoules — check concentration (10-fold error risk).
drugs.renalHepatic: Active metabolite accumulates in renal failure; prolonged effect in hepatic failure and elderly.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid
drugs.indications: Trauma patients with significant haemorrhage within 3 h of injury (including mass casualty incidents)
drugs.adultDose: 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h; give within 3 h of injury (CRASH-2).
drugs.preparationIndia: 500 mg/5 mL ampoules widely available and inexpensive.
drugs.cautions: No benefit (possible harm) if started >3 h after injury; seizures at high doses.
